week.t: Perseverance measures Mars dust clinging to spacesuit swatches
PACE satellite maps autumn leaves turning red across the north
Swift ends after 22 years; re-entry within weeks
Dragonfly completes its first simulated flight
Three mosquito species pick different people

tiles.cap: Mars dust clings to spacesuit cloth for years. Perseverance measured grains 100 nm wide.
tiles.nums: Martian days of dust measurements on five spacesuit swatches riding on Perseverance
tiles.p1: Perseverance carries five squares of spacesuit material, each 20 mm across, on the calibration target of its SHERLOC instrument. Over 1,645 Martian days the rover’s PIXL X-ray instrument measured the dust that settled on them and on PIXL’s own Teflon and basaltic-glass targets. It found fine particles below 2.5 micrometres and ultrafine ones around 100 nanometres, far smaller than the roughly 3 micrometres earlier Mars measurements could resolve.
tiles.p2: Published Tuesday 27 October in PNAS; lead author Scott VanBommel of Washington University in St. Louis. The findings feed into spacesuit and habitat design, dust-removal procedures and crew health standards.
deep: Static decides what sticks

Grains pick up charge as they collide in the Martian air, and static electricity appears to decide which sizes stick to which surfaces. On PIXL’s Teflon target and SHERLOC’s Vectran swatch, particles averaged about 2 micrometres; on PIXL’s basaltic glass and SHERLOC’s Teflon swatch, sizes ran down to 100 to 300 nanometres. The finest grains stayed put through years of driving and drilling.
Why size matters for lungs

On Earth, particles below 2.5 micrometres reach deep into the lungs and can enter the bloodstream. Ultrafine particles of 100 nanometres or less can travel from the nasal cavity to the brain along the olfactory nerve. Martian dust is mostly silicate minerals and includes perchlorates, which can disrupt thyroid function, and reactive iron, which can damage cells. The risk is thought to depend on how much dust and for how long.
What is in it

Chemically the dust matches the iron- and sulfur-rich composition earlier missions measured, and PIXL found it enriched in phosphorus, with signs of calcium sulfate. Mars grains are less abrasive than Moon dust, which during Apollo scratched visors, wore outer suit layers, damaged seals and gave some crew members hay-fever-like symptoms.
Designing around it

Some materials hold less dust than others, which could guide future material and coating choices. Suitports and dual-chamber airlocks could cut how much dust gets into living quarters. In March 2025 NASA tested an Electrodynamic Dust Shield on the Moon aboard Firefly Aerospace’s Blue Ghost Mission 1, using electric fields to clear regolith from glass and radiator surfaces.

tiles.cap: NASA’s Titan drone flew its whole first flight on a computer that believes it is on Titan.
tiles.nums: arrival at Titan, after launch no earlier than 2028 and a six-year voyage
tiles.p1: Dragonfly is the rotorcraft NASA will send to Saturn’s moon Titan. In a blog post on Friday 23 October NASA said the team at Johns Hopkins APL in Laurel, Maryland had run its simulated first flight, from backshell separation to landing, in real time on flight-like avionics, the most comprehensive test of that flight so far. The computer flew on simulated data from Dragonfly’s navigation cameras, inertial measurement units and lidar, covering most of the systems and manoeuvres it will use on Titan.
tiles.p2: Titan is too far for anyone on Earth to steer it live, so Dragonfly must fly itself. Next: the same flight on the real flight system, other flight profiles, and faults injected on purpose to confirm it recovers on its own.
deep: Built up one rotor at a time
The team tested incrementally: first a single rotor spinning, then a short reposition flight, then a partial scouting flight, adding sensors at each step.
Faking Titan for the cameras
A custom camera emulator renders Titan scenes on GPUs and matches the 20 to 70 millisecond exposure times of the real cameras, so the flight computer sees what it would see over the dunes.
Three years of hopping
Dragonfly launches no earlier than 2028, travels for six years and arrives in 2034. It then spends three years flying between sites on Titan.
Lowering it out of the shell

Lockheed Martin engineers are testing the mechanism that lowers the rotorcraft from its stowed position inside the backshell into position for release during descent: static load tests, deployment tests, and deployments at tilted angles.

tiles.cap: Built for 2 years, Swift watched for 22 and caught 2,000 explosions. Now it falls.
tiles.nums: targets a day Swift could schedule, swinging to a new gamma-ray burst within about a minute
tiles.p1: NASA’s Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory has ended its science mission. It has sunk below 275 km, where atmospheric drag is too strong for its telescopes to hold steady on a target, and it made its final observation on 20 October. Designed for a two-year primary phase, it worked more than ten times that long: over 2,000 gamma-ray bursts, more than 1,400 supernovae, stars shredded by black holes, an all-sky X-ray survey, asteroids and comets.
tiles.p2: Re-entry is expected within a few weeks. Its public archive is about 12 terabytes, including more than 1.5 million images from its ultraviolet/optical telescope, and has fed about 7,000 papers.
deep: The one-minute pivot

Principal investigator S. Bradley Cenko describes the job: detect a gamma-ray burst, share its position, and turn the telescopes to image it before the afterglow fades, typically within about a minute. Flexible scheduling let astronomers request rapid target-of-opportunity observations, up to 75 targets a day.
The 2005 catch

In May 2005 Swift detected the afterglow of GRB 050509B, the first short gamma-ray burst ever seen with an afterglow. Those observations supported the idea that short bursts come from two neutron stars merging.
Launched 2004, renamed 2018
Swift launched on 20 November 2004. NASA renamed it in 2018 after Neil Gehrels, its first principal investigator, following his death. Nearly 22 years of data sit in the archive.
What fills the gap

Shawn Domagal-Goldman, director of NASA’s Astrophysics Division, says Swift delivered an incredible, lasting return on investment. NASA says it will use current missions to respond rapidly to cosmic events while it looks for new ways to do so.

tiles.cap: Apple’s folding iPhone is 5.2 mm thin open. The crease is there; you just can’t see it.
tiles.nums: thickness of the iPhone Duo open; 11.3 mm closed; 254 grams
tiles.p1: The iPhone Duo folds a 7.6-inch OLED screen (1878 by 2670 pixels, 430 ppi) into a passport-sized phone with a 5.4-inch outer display. Open, it is 5.2 mm thick; closed, 11.3 mm; it weighs 254 grams. The hinge cover is 3D-printed from 100% recycled titanium, the enclosure is 85% recycled titanium, and the glass is Ceramic Shield 2 on the front and Ceramic Shield on the back.
tiles.p2: TIME Best Inventions 2026. US$1,999 for 256 GB, Apple’s most expensive iPhone. TechRadar’s verdict: a fully realised folding iPhone, but Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8 is lighter, thinner and slightly cheaper.
deep: Hiding the crease

Every folding screen creases where it bends. Apple’s fix is the top layer: a matte nano-texture finish on the inner display that scatters light where the crease would show. TechRadar’s Lance Ulanoff cannot see it but can still feel it with a finger. Beneath sit custom polymer sheets, the OLED panel, a couple of glass layers and a titanium backing, bonded with flexible glue so the layers can slide as the phone folds.
The hinge

TIME reports more than 100 tiny components inside the hinge. Ulanoff says it is satisfying to use and essentially disappears when the phone is open flat. Apple’s new CEO John Ternus and five other engineers filed a patent application for foldable devices back in 2011.
The numbers inside

A20 Pro chip: Geekbench 7.1 scores of 4,007 single-core and 11,363 multi-core. Both screens run at 120 Hz and up to 3,000 nits. Apple quotes up to 44 hours of video on the outer screen and 31 on the inner; TechRadar got about 14 hours of real-world use and 13 in lab testing, and a 45 W charger reached 60% in 30 minutes. Rated IP68, 6 metres for 30 minutes; the reviewer held it under a running tap.
What reviewers found wrong

254 g is about 53 g heavier than the Galaxy Z Fold 8 and nearly 2 mm thicker folded. No Face ID, only Touch ID. The 2x zoom is a crop of the 48 MP sensor, not a true telephoto lens. Some apps look stretched on the inner screen, the right-side dock on the cover screen will divide opinion, and 256 GB is thin at this price. Apple Pencil support was still to come.
tiles.src: Apple tech specs · TechRadar review, 21 Oct 2026 · TIME Best Inventions 2026

tiles.cap: A satellite named for plankton is now tracking autumn leaves turning red, worldwide.
tiles.nums: colour bands PACE’s Ocean Color Instrument sees in; a few groups of them track leaf pigments
tiles.p1: NASA’s PACE satellite scans the planet daily across 286 spectral bands. Scientists use it to follow three leaf pigments, anthocyanins (reds), carotenoids (yellows and oranges) and chlorophylls (greens), and score autumn colour as the ratio of red, orange and yellow to green. A value near 1 means most leaves have not turned yet.
tiles.p2: From 29 September to 4 October the reddest places were northern and eastern Russia, northern Alaska and northern Canada. By 5 to 11 October the red had moved south into the Mid-Atlantic, Mongolia and northern China.
deep: What the map can fool you with
Not every red or yellow pixel is autumn foliage. Some farmland, clouds, and drought or insect stress change the readings too.
The ground truth

Landsat 9 caught red and orange ridges around Ripton, Vermont on 3 October, near the regional peak, in Vermont’s Green Mountains, rich in sugar maples and red maples. A GLOBE volunteer photographed leaves in Meredith, New Hampshire on 11 October. NASA data scientist Skye Caplan posts weekly PACE foliage maps and says the more ground photos, the better.
Slowly, then all at once

Caplan: “Color changes happen kind of slowly, then all at once, and then they’re gone.” Karl Huemmrich of the University of Maryland, Baltimore County calls a repeated worldwide time series of anthocyanins and carotenoids game-changing.
Why bother
Ground data checks the satellite, and the same pigment tracking can watch spring greening, the carbon cycle, wildfire risk, and early signs of drought, insect damage and plant disease.

tiles.cap: Three mosquito species each have favourite humans. Nobody was the favourite of all three.
tiles.nums: volunteers sniffed by three mosquito species, without a single bite
tiles.p1: Some people get bitten far more than others. Researchers at Florida International University, led by Kaylee Marrero with Matthew DeGennaro, let caged Aedes aegypti, Aedes albopictus and Culex quinquefasciatus smell the arms of 119 volunteers through a device that stops them biting, and counted how many approached each person’s scent. Each species preferred a different mix of people, and no one was the favourite of all three.
tiles.p2: Mosquitoes spread dengue and Zika, so knowing whom they pick could help prevent disease. Published in iScience on 21 August 2026; reported by Science News Explores on Friday.
deep: Day biters, night biters
The two Aedes species bite by day, so volunteers came to the lab. Culex bites at night, so volunteers wore nylon sleeves for several hours and the sleeves went into the device after dark.
What the chemistry said

The team sampled the air around each arm. Aedes aegypti and Culex quinquefasciatus were drawn to people with less skin odour. Aedes albopictus went for 13 chemicals that smell like plants. Human scent can involve more than 1,000 chemicals, so some may have been missed.
The bacteria everyone shares
Certain skin bacteria attracted all three species. Marrero’s group next wants to work out how those bacteria make the smelly compounds.
Why species differ
Possible reasons include which animals each species normally feeds on and what time of day it feeds. The findings could guide new repellents, including microbe-based ones, or scented lures for traps.

tiles.cap: Three voters can make a loop: A beats B, B beats C, C beats A. Underneath: a Klein bottle.
tiles.nums: when Condorcet found the paradox; in 1951 Arrow proved no ranking method escapes it
tiles.p1: Split voters into three equal groups. One ranks Alice, Bob, Carol; the next Bob, Carol, Alice; the last Carol, Alice, Bob. Alice beats Bob two groups to one, Bob beats Carol, and Carol beats Alice. Every voter is perfectly consistent, yet the group’s choice runs in a circle. Nicolas de Condorcet found this in 1785, and in 1951 Kenneth Arrow proved that no ranking method can satisfy four reasonable rules at once.
tiles.p2: In 2025 Ori Livson and Mikhail Prokopenko at the University of Sydney, with Siddharth Pritam of the Chennai Mathematical Institute, showed the paradox lives on a Klein bottle: a one-sided surface with no inside, no outside and no edge.
deep: Check it yourself

Take the three rankings above and compare each pair. Alice vs Bob: groups 1 and 3 prefer Alice. Bob vs Carol: groups 1 and 2 prefer Bob. Carol vs Alice: groups 2 and 3 prefer Carol. Three majorities, one loop.
Ballots as triangles

In 1993 Yuliy Baryshnikov drew each of the six possible rankings as a triangle, one corner for each pairwise comparison. Rankings that agree on two comparisons share an edge, so the six triangles glue into a strip, and the strip’s matching ends bend round into a tube. That tube gave a topological proof of Arrow’s theorem.
The rims he ignored

One rim of the tube reads Alice over Bob, Bob over Carol, Carol over Alice; the other runs the cycle backwards. Both are Condorcet loops. Gluing the rims straight pairs up incompatible rankings; gluing with a twist works. Livson: “Gluing with the twist is the only valid option.” Twist a strip and join it and you get a Möbius strip; twist a tube and join it and you get a Klein bottle.
Arrow’s four rules

Voters may rank candidates in any order. No single voter dictates the outcome. If everyone prefers one option to another, the group ranking agrees. And how two candidates rank should depend only on how voters compare those two. Iain McLean of Oxford: “It’s not really a mathematical debate. It’s a debate about values.”

tiles.cap: Monday’s PSI fell to 67–74. Today’s forecast: 60–90, showers, haze unlikely.
tiles.p1: Monday was cloudy over Singapore. At 6pm the 1-hour PM2.5 was 28 to 40 µg/m³, Band 1 (Normal), and the 24-hour PSI 67 to 74, Moderate, down from 91 to 107 on Sunday. Smoke haze was visible on satellite over Kalimantan but stayed there.
tiles.p2: For Tuesday NEA expects winds from the northeast or southeast and showers over Singapore and nearby, so haze is unlikely to affect us.
deep: The wind has swung

Sunday’s update had Monday’s wind from the southwest or west. Monday’s update has it from the northeast or southeast for Tuesday, then variable on Wednesday and Thursday with showers. NEA says the wet weather should keep hotspot and smoke haze activity suppressed.
Two numbers, two jobs

Use the PSI forecast to plan tomorrow’s outdoor activities; for right now, check the 1-hour PM2.5 on NEA’s haze site or the myENV app. How much the haze affects you depends on your health, the PSI level, and how long and how hard you are active outdoors.
What the satellite could not see
Cloud cover again stopped NEA from determining the full extent of the hotspots and haze. Lighter haze does not show up clearly from satellite.
The week in numbers
Sunday 91–107, Moderate to Unhealthy. Monday 67–74, Moderate. Tuesday forecast 60–90, Moderate.

tiles.cap: Haunted houses may hum below 20 hertz. You can’t hear it, but your spit knows.
tiles.nums: infrasound, below the lower limit of human hearing
tiles.p1: Infrasound is sound below 20 hertz, too low to hear. Volcanoes and earthquakes make it; so do traffic, trains and air conditioning, and possibly the old plumbing and air ducts of supposedly haunted buildings. Behavioural neuroscientist Kale Scatterty at the University of Alberta had 36 people, all college students, listen to music, half of them with two subwoofers outside the room playing infrasound. The infrasound group rated the music sadder and less interesting, reported more irritability, and had more cortisol, a stress marker, in their saliva.
tiles.p2: They could not reliably tell whether they had been exposed. Scatterty says infrasound seems to affect mood and biology without people being conscious of it. Halloween is this Saturday.
deep: The setup

Two rooms had speakers for music, either a soothing spa-like track or an eerie horror-film tune. The subwoofers for the infrasound sat outside the rooms. Participants rated the music and their feelings, gave saliva samples, and afterwards guessed whether infrasound had been on.
How you might sense it

One possibility: the otolith organs in the ear, which sense movement and position, might pick up vibrations too low to hear. Earlier work suggested animals may detect infrasound with their bodies and that it might provoke anxiety or fear.
What it did not do

Nobody reported feeling scared or anxious. Scatterty admits the mood effect could come from the setup itself: “It could have very well just been that we were priming them to feel something.” The students might also have been irritable because they had other places to be.
Next

Long-term effects are unknown; cities with heavy infrastructure may be most exposed. The team has considered running the same measurements in a Halloween haunted house. Published 27 April 2026 in Frontiers in Behavioral Neuroscience.

tiles.cap: NASA's next giant telescope passed checkout. It sees 100 million times fainter than you.
tiles.nums: fainter than the human eye can see: Roman’s Wide Field Instrument
tiles.p1: The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope has finished its checkout and moved into science commissioning: test observations that calibrate its instruments and sharpen image quality before real science begins. Senior project scientist Julie McEnery says the observatory is fully functional. NASA adds that some systems are performing even better than required.
tiles.p2: Last Thursday’s update. Meanwhile Hubble has been photographing gravitational lenses to get Roman’s map ready.
deep: The crowded-field worry
One concern was that Roman’s guidance system might struggle to lock onto stars in crowded star fields and dusty nebulae. Operations project scientist Tom Barclay reports those tests went well.
Why tiny flaws matter

Josh Schlieder, the Wide Field Instrument scientist, says image flaws must be minimised because small imperfections could hide faint signals. The instrument can detect objects about a hundred million times fainter than the human eye can see.
Hubble is drawing the map

Hubble photographs one gravitational lens at a time; Roman’s much wider view should catch a far larger sample. Astronomers are using Hubble’s sharp images to build a computer model for analysing Roman’s big pictures, and Hubble will follow up on the interesting lenses Roman finds.
What a lens tells you

In one Hubble image, an elliptical galaxy about 4.5 billion light-years away bends the light of a galaxy about 8 billion light-years away into an arc, with a smaller flipped copy on the other side. Visible matter cannot account for the bending, so the distortion lets researchers work out how much dark matter the foreground galaxy holds.

tiles.cap: NASA’s Psyche is crossing to the asteroid belt with its engines on nearly 90% of the time.
tiles.nums: of thrust from xenon ion engines, running nearly 90% of the time until 2029
tiles.p1: After a Mars gravity assist, Psyche has fired its electric thrusters nearly non-stop since 28 September, pausing once a week to check in with Earth. The Hall-effect thrusters push with up to 250 millinewtons by firing out xenon ions, and navigation lead Don Han says they will run nearly 90% of the time until arrival.
tiles.p2: Target: a metal-rich asteroid about 280 km across thought to be the partial core of a planetesimal, a building block of an early planet. Orbit by summer 2029.
deep: Fuel
It launched in October 2023 with about 1,090 kg of xenon and has used roughly a third in three years.
Powered by sunlight

Two five-panel solar arrays with 75 square metres of collecting area run the thrusters. Propulsion engineer Steve Snyder says they fire at full power for three months, then throttle down to about half as sunlight weakens further out.
The twist problem
The swirling ions give the spacecraft a slight twisting force. Reaction wheels absorb it, and periodic manoeuvres dump the built-up momentum.
Why Mars first

Principal investigator Lindy Elkins-Tanton says the Mars flyby let the team calibrate instruments and rehearse for the asteroid encounter. Her line: “cruising with confidence deeper into the solar system, powered by sunlight”.

tiles.cap: Ingenuity flew 0.7 km in one go. New blades could take a Mars helicopter 18.7 km.
tiles.nums: in one uninterrupted flight, carrying scientific instruments
tiles.p1: NASA Ames, with Imperial College London and Nagoya University, designed a thinner, asymmetrical rotor blade shape called roamx-0201 using simulations tuned to Mars conditions. In wind tunnel tests it performed better and recovered better in risky flight conditions. Ingenuity, the first powered aircraft on another planet, could cover 0.7 km in one flight; the new blades could stretch that to as much as 18.7 km.
tiles.p2: Paper published 22 September. Not Mars-ready yet: engineers are still closing the gap between what the computer predicts and what the wind tunnel shows.
deep: The speed-of-sound wall
The speed of sound is lower on Mars than on Earth, so rotor tips approach it sooner and performance drops suddenly. The new blades run longer at higher speeds before that happens.
Tripping the air on purpose
The airfoil deliberately disrupts the boundary layer of air at its leading edge, which NASA says lifts the rotorcraft more effectively than earlier designs.
Stall
Ingenuity’s blades lost performance steeply at stall. Under the conditions tested, roamx-0201 behaved much better, which could let future helicopters fly safely across a wider range of angles.
What flies next
SkyFall, due to launch in 2028, carries three helicopters to Mars with curved-edge blades like Ingenuity’s. The new shape is meant for the missions after that.

tiles.cap: A drone that lands on the sea, flips itself upright, and follows you at 55 km/h
tiles.nums: how low it flies above the waves
tiles.p1: The HoverAir Aqua is a 249-gram camera drone built for surfers and paddlers. It floats, takes off from water, and rights itself if a wave flips it. Instead of a controller it follows a small wristband, and a radar pointing straight down measures the height of each wave so it can skim half a metre above the surface.
tiles.p2: Named one of TIME's Best Inventions of 2026. About US$1,300.
deep: How it knows where you are

Cameras on most drones lose a person against moving water. This one tracks the wristband by radio, using RTK, the same correction trick that lets survey GPS reach centimetre accuracy instead of metres. The drone always knows exactly where the band is, even if it cannot see you.
Why the radar

Water's surface is never still, so a normal height sensor would read nonsense. A millimetre-wave radar reads the wave height many times a second and the drone adjusts, which is how it holds 50 cm without clipping a crest.
The weight is not an accident
249 g is one gram under the 250 g line where many countries' drone rules get stricter. The engineers designed to that number.
What reviewers found

It really does take off and land on water and the self-righting works. Weak points: tracking sometimes crops your head, a single water drop on the lens ruins a shot, and 23 minutes of battery goes fast. 4K at 100 frames a second from a 1/1.28-inch sensor.
tiles.src: HoverAir official specs · TechRadar review · TIME Best Inventions 2026

tiles.cap: Stare at this and your eyes will invent a colour
tiles.p1: Your three colour sensors tire out separately. Wear out green, look at white, and you see a magenta ghost. That's an afterimage.
tiles.p2: Then mix red, green and blue light yourself in the PhET simulator.
deep: What's happening in your eye

Your retina has three kinds of cone cells, roughly for red, green and blue. Stare at one colour and the cones for it get fatigued and fire less. Look at white, and the other two shout louder, so you see the opposite colour.
The test
Look at the white dot in the green disc for 30 seconds without moving your eyes. Then look at a blank white wall. You should see a magenta disc that follows your gaze and fades over several seconds.
Try variations
Stare at red and you see cyan. Stare at blue and you see yellow. Half-cover the shape and the ghost has a hard edge. Blink and it jumps.
Mix light yourself
Red + green light = yellow. All three = white. Your screen does this with every pixel.

tiles.cap: Thirty learning scientists agreed on one rule: think first, ask second
tiles.p1: Thirty learning scientists were asked when AI helps learning and when it hurts. Their answer was not good or bad. They called it the GenAI Paradox: AI is strong at helping you consolidate what you already know, and weak, sometimes harmful, when you use it to learn something new or to do the hard thinking.
tiles.p2: Their one-line rule: do your own first attempt, then bring in the AI.
deep: Use it for

Testing yourself after you have learned something. Feedback on your own draft. Widening your options after you have written down your own ideas. Asking it to attack your reasoning and find the weak spot.
Don't use it for
Learning a topic from scratch. Writing the essay or doing the problem set for you. Skipping the struggle, because the struggle is where learning happens.
The caveat they added
Most research on this is still young, so these are expert judgments, not settled facts. Watch how your own memory behaves and update.
tiles.src: University of Minnesota CEHD, expert consensus report, Oct 2026
